title: High-level and low-level languages
specPoints: 2.5.1 Characteristics and purpose of different levels of programming language: **high-level** and **low-level** (machine code and assembly)
Advantages and disadvantages of each; when each is used
learn: Describe machine code, assembly language and high-level languages and place them on a scale
Give two characteristics of high-level and of low-level languages
Explain why most programs are written in high-level languages and when low-level is chosen
Explain the terms portable, mnemonic, processor-specific, and human-readable in context
Read a short assembly fragment and say what it does (in outline)
hook: Here is the same instruction three ways: `total = price + vat` · `ADD R1, R2, R3` · `10110010 00011100`. Which would you rather write? Which does the processor actually understand? Everything in between is translation — and that is lesson 2.

video.title: Three levels, one instruction
video.brief: 3 minutes. A single addition shown as Python, then assembly (mnemonic ADD with registers), then binary machine code, sliding down a 'closeness to hardware' scale. Annotate each with its characteristics: human-readable / portable vs processor-specific / fast / memory-efficient. End with the two situations where low-level wins: device drivers and embedded systems with tight memory and timing.

explain.code:
HIGH-LEVEL     Python, Java, C#, JavaScript        total = price + vat
     |         close to human language; one line does a lot; portable
     |
LOW-LEVEL      Assembly language                    ADD R1, R2, R3
     |         mnemonics for processor instructions; one line = one instruction
     |
               Machine code                         10110010 00011100 ...
               binary the CPU executes directly; processor-specific

list: Written in something close to English with maths-style expressions; **easy to read, write and debug**.
**Portable**: the same source code can be translated to run on different processors.
One statement does many machine-level steps, so programs are **shorter** and faster to write.
Must be **translated** (compiled or interpreted) before the CPU can run it (lesson 2).
Programmer has **less direct control** of memory and hardware; translated code may be larger or slower than hand-written low-level code.
**Machine code** is binary; the CPU runs it directly with no translation. Almost nobody writes it by hand.
**Assembly language** uses short **mnemonics** (`ADD`, `LDA`, `JMP`) for each machine instruction, plus names for registers and memory. An **assembler** translates it 1-to-1 into machine code.
**Processor-specific**: written for one CPU family; not portable.
Gives **direct control** of hardware and memory; can be very **fast** and **small**.
**Hard to write and debug**; long programs; needs knowledge of the CPU's architecture.

p: High-level for almost everything: apps, websites, games, data analysis — where programmer time matters more than squeezing the last microsecond. Low-level where control of hardware is essential: **device drivers**, **embedded systems** (1.1.3) with tiny memory, **real-time** control, the heart of an operating system, and performance-critical sections of games or scientific code.

explain.code:
LDA 10      ; load the value at memory address 10 into the accumulator
ADD 11      ; add the value at address 11
STA 12      ; store the result at address 12
HLT         ; stop
after: That is `c = a + b` in four instructions. You are not expected to write assembly at GCSE, but you should recognise that each line is one tiny step and uses mnemonics — the Little Man Computer simulator in the Try section makes this concrete.

list: **High-level** (Python): looks like English and maths. Easy to write. Works on any computer after translation.
**Assembly**: short codes like `ADD` and `LDA`, one per processor step. Hard to write. Only for one type of processor.
**Machine code**: the 1s and 0s the processor actually runs.

p: High-level: quick to write and fix, portable, but needs translating and gives less control.
Low-level: fast, small, full control of the hardware, but slow to write, hard to debug, not portable.
People writing device drivers, tiny embedded systems, and the very core of operating systems.

keyterms.def: A programming language close to human language, independent of a specific processor, that must be translated to run.
Machine code or assembly language, close to the hardware and specific to a processor.
Binary instructions executed directly by the CPU.
A low-level language using mnemonics for machine instructions; translated by an assembler.
A short memorable code for an instruction, e.g. ADD, LDA.
Able to run on different types of computer/processor after translation.

try.title: 1. Little Man Computer: write assembly
instructions: Enter the four-line program from the lesson (LDA, ADD, STA, HLT) with two numbers in memory and step through it. Watch the accumulator.
Now write a program that inputs two numbers and outputs the larger. Count the instructions. Then write the same thing in Python below.

try.title: 2. The same program, high-level
p: Write 'input two numbers, output the larger'. Compare line count and readability with your LMC version. Which took longer to write? Which would be easier to fix in a month?

try.title: 3. Sort the statements
p: Put each under High-level or Low-level: portable · processor-specific · uses mnemonics · one line does many steps · needs a compiler or interpreter · runs directly on the CPU · easier to debug · direct control of memory · used for device drivers · used for web apps.

try.title: 4. Choose and justify
p: For each, say high- or low-level and give two reasons: (a) a mobile banking app; (b) the firmware in a pacemaker; (c) a school's timetable software; (d) the driver for a new graphics card; (e) a data-analysis script run once.

try.title: 5. Fetch–decode–execute
instructions: Link to Paper 1: watch each assembly instruction go through fetch, decode, execute. Machine code is what the decode step reads.

opts: Can be translated to run on different processors

check.q: The only language a CPU runs directly is:
A reason to use a low-level language:
opts: Direct control of hardware and memory

exam.q: Describe **two** characteristics of a high-level programming language.
model: Any two: uses English-like keywords / is easy for humans to read and write (1); is portable across different processors (1); one statement translates into many machine code instructions (1); must be translated before it can run (1).
exam.commentary: Characteristics, not advantages: 'it is better' scores nothing.

exam.q: A company is writing software to control a washing machine with a very small amount of memory. Explain why a low-level language might be chosen.
model: Low-level code gives direct control of the hardware/memory (1), producing smaller and faster programs than translated high-level code (1), which matters when memory is very limited / timing is critical in an embedded system (1).
exam.commentary: Tie each point to the scenario: small memory, embedded control.

exam.q: State **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of writing a program in assembly language rather than a high-level language.
model: Advantage: faster execution / smaller / direct hardware control (1). Disadvantage: harder and slower to write and debug / not portable (1).

home: Find out which language the operating system on your phone or laptop is mostly written in, and which language a game or app you use is written in. For each, write two sentences on why that level of language makes sense.

extension.title: Beyond GCSE — A-level extension (optional): addressing modes and the instruction set

p: At A-level you learn how an assembly instruction is encoded: an **opcode** (the operation) and an **operand** (the data or address), and the different **addressing modes** — immediate (`ADD #5`: the 5 itself), direct (`ADD 5`: the contents of address 5), indirect and indexed. Try in the LMC: find out whether `ADD 5` adds 5 or adds what is stored at mailbox 5. Then look up the LMC's instruction set and work out how many bits the opcode and operand take in its 3-digit code.

teacher.timing: 60 min: hook 3 · explain 12 · try 28 · check 5 · exam 9 · homework 3
misconceptions: 'Low-level' heard as 'bad' or 'basic'. It means close to the hardware.
Assembly and machine code treated as the same thing. Assembly is the mnemonic form; the assembler makes machine code.
Believing high-level programs run without translation.
Thinking portability means the compiled program runs anywhere — it is the *source* that is portable.
say: 'Low means close to the metal, not low quality.'
'One Python line, ten assembly lines, ten machine-code instructions.'
teacher.skip: Try 5 is a Paper 1 bridge; cut before Try 1–3.
differentiation: Support: Try 3 as a card sort.
Stretch: the extension on addressing modes using the LMC.
